records.toxicity_detail: Toxic to cats, sharing the same acute-kidney-injury pattern documented for true lilies. UF/IFAS's dedicated Daylily toxicity write-up (EP648) states: "All parts of the plant are toxic to dogs and cats. Even a small amount of plant material can cause serious concerns if ingested. The mechanism of the toxicity is still unknown, but it is known to cause acute kidney injury in cats. Symptoms include gastrointestinal irritation, followed by dehydration, vomiting, and then renal failure. Seizures can also occur in some cases." NC State's Hemerocallis genus page adds that affected cats "may show signs of vomiting, inappetence, lethargy, kidney failure, and even death after eating." NC State's own Hemerocallis fulva species page ("The plant is reportedly toxic to cats"), the RHS species page ("TOXIC to pets (cats)"), and UGA CAES ("Major Toxicity (for cats)") all independently confirm cat toxicity for this species. Sources disagree on dogs specifically -- NC State tags H. fulva "non-toxic for dogs" while UF/IFAS EP648 says all parts are toxic to dogs and cats -- so this record asserts toxicity for cats only, where every source is unanimous.

records.name_note: Two admissible sources anchor to different accepted names and neither resolves to the other's. NC State Extension's own page is titled "Ceropegia woodii" and states "Previously known as: Ceropegia linearis subsp. woodii" -- treating Ceropegia woodii as the current name and Ceropegia linearis subsp. woodii as the superseded one. RHS's own page is titled "Ceropegia linearis subsp. woodii," carries a structured "Name Status: Correct" tag for that binomial, and lists "Ceropegia woodii" among its Synonyms -- treating Ceropegia linearis subsp. woodii as the accepted name and Ceropegia woodii as a synonym of it. Because the two sources take opposite positions on which of the two names is currently accepted, scientific_name_accepted is left null rather than picking a side.
records.cool_rest_note: NC State: "It is dormant over the winter and watering should be reduced even further." RHS's cultivation guidance describes the same growing-season/rest-season split: "Water moderately when in growth and apply a low nitrogen liquid fertiliser 2 or 3 times. Keep plants dry at other times."
records.water_dry_down_target: Let the soil dry out completely between waterings. NC State: "Be careful not to overwater this plant. It should be allowed to dry out completely between waterings."
unknowns: toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail: left null. NC State Extension's Ceropegia woodii page does carry a structured 'Poisonous to Humans' block (Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: 'Vomiting (sometimes with blood), diarrhea, depression'; Poison Toxic Principle: 'Lectin, wisterin glycoside'; Poison Part: Bark, Flowers, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds), but I verified by independently fetching NC State's own Wisteria sinensis page (https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/wisteria-sinensis/) that this exact block -- identical severity, identical symptom text, and identical 'wisterin glycoside' toxic principle (a compound name derived from Wisteria, not Ceropegia) and 'Bark' listed as a poisoned part, which makes no botanical sense for a non-woody succulent vine -- is reproduced byte-for-byte on that unrelated species' page too. This is a templating/caching defect on NC State's site, not species-specific data, so it was excluded rather than used for toxicity in either direction. Separately, that block is headed 'Poisonous to Humans,' not pets, so per the task's own rule it could not have supported toxic_to_pets even if genuine. RHS's page has zero occurrences of toxic/poison/harmful/irritant anywhere in its HTML, so no admissible source actually addresses toxicity -- to pets or otherwise -- for this species.

day_f_min/day_f_max and night_f_min/night_f_max: left null. Neither source states an indoor or outdoor day/night temperature range for this species; NC State's page contains no temperature figures at all, and RHS gives only a categorical outdoor hardiness rating (see chill_damage_f note), not a day/night range.

chill_damage_f: left null. RHS rates this species 'H1C,' but the accompanying explanatory text -- 'can be grown outside in the summer (5 - 10)' -- is part of RHS's site-wide Hardiness Ratings legend (H1A through H7) that is reused verbatim across every RHS plant page, not a species-specific damage-onset temperature. It is also framed as an outdoor-growing-suitability window, not a stated point where sublethal chill damage begins, so it was not converted into a Fahrenheit damage-onset figure.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: left null. Neither admissible source mentions humidity for this species at all.
light_fc_min and light_fc_good: left null. Neither source gives a foot-candle light figure for this species.

records.name_note: All three admissible sources consulted -- NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder, and RHS -- consistently use Dionaea muscipula as both the given and the accepted binomial. No conflicting accepted name was found for this species.
records.water_dry_down_target: Never allow the soil to dry out -- keep it constantly/permanently wet, ideally with the pot standing in a saucer or tray of water. Use only rainwater, distilled water, or reverse-osmosis water; ordinary tap water (chlorinated or hard) can kill the plant.
unknowns: night_f_min / night_f_max: no admissible source gives a distinct nighttime temperature figure for the active growing season; RHS's "10–27°C (50–80°F)" range (used for day_f_min/day_f_max) is a single undifferentiated range, not split into day vs. night.

chill_damage_f: left null on a genuine conflict. RHS instructs keeping a potted plant "above 10°C/50°F" during its winter rest ("Avoid keeping in a warm room over winter – it needs a cool rest (but above 10°C/50°F)"), while Missouri Botanical Garden recommends overwintering containers indoors "in a sunny but cool area (southern window) with temperatures of 40-50 degrees F" — explicitly endorsing temperatures below RHS's stated floor for the same practical scenario (a potted plant's indoor winter rest). Neither side was adopted.
humidity_pct_min / humidity_pct_max: no admissible source gives a percentage figure, only NC State's categorical "high humidity" (captured in humidity_need).
light_fc_min / light_fc_good: no admissible source gives footcandle figures for this species.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's "6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day" is a sitewide generic definition of its "Full sun" category label used across all Plant Toolbox species pages, not a species-specific sun-hours ceiling for Dionaea muscipula, so it was not used to populate this field.

soil_base: the recommended media — "whole-fiber sphagnum moss" or "equal parts peat moss and coarse vermiculite or sharp sand" (NC State), "sustainably grown live sphagnum moss or peat-free carnivorous plant compost" (RHS), "a mixture of sand and peat moss" (Missouri Botanical Garden) — does not cleanly match any fixed soil_base enum option, so it is left null rather than forced into an awkward fit (cactus_succulent or semi_hydro would both misrepresent a peat/sphagnum bog mix).

soil_ph_min: NC State's structured field gives only an upper bound, "Acid (<6.0)"; no admissible source gives an explicit lower-bound pH number, so soil_ph_min is left null while soil_ph_max is set to 6.0.

water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a numeric watering-interval, check-depth, or dormancy-duration figure; all three sources describe watering qualitatively ("never let dry out", "kept permanently wet", pot standing in a saucer of water) rather than as a check-and-water schedule.

fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: left null by design, not by data gap. NC State is explicit — "Do not fertilize the plant" — consistent with the species note that it derives nitrogen from digested insect prey rather than soil/fertilizer, so no fertilizing schedule applies at all.

toxicity_detail: left null. NC State's page carries only the categorical tags "#non-toxic for cats", "#non-toxic for horses", and "#non-toxic for dogs", with no prose describing a mechanism or symptom set to summarize into a detail field.

is_houseplant is set true on NC State's structured "Houseplant" Plant Type tag/Landscape Location listing and RHS's "It is relatively easy to grow as a houseplant." Missouri Botanical Garden is notably more cautious on this exact question without flatly contradicting it — "Growth as a houseplant is possible but can be difficult because of the need for growing season sun, humidity and winter dormancy" and "Plants often do not grow well as houseplants" — so the true value is kept, but this is not an easy-care tropical foliage plant indoors and that caveat should travel with the field.

No schema field cleanly captures the plant's single most safety-critical care fact — that ordinary tap water can kill it. NC State: "treated (chlorinated) water or hard water can kill the plant"; RHS: "tap water, especially in hard water areas, can kill it"; Missouri Botanical Garden: "It is best to use rain water, distilled water, or reverse osmosis water." This is captured in water_dry_down_target in the absence of a dedicated water-source/water-quality field.
scientific_name_accepted: no conflict found — NC State, Missouri Botanical Garden, and RHS all consistently use Dionaea muscipula as both the given and the accepted name.

cool_rest_note — removed on audit: The field asserts RHS instructs 'avoiding a warm room,' but the citations array's RHS entry for cool_rest_note only quotes 'Give it a cooler rest period over winter' -- it does not include the warm-room language. I fetched the live RHS page and confirmed RHS really does say 'Avoid keeping in a warm room over winter - it needs a cool rest (but above 10 C/50 F),' so the claim is factually accurate, but that supporting quote was never entered into the citations array under any claim label. As constructed, this specific clause in the field's own value fails structural check 1 (every non-null field value must trace to an entry in citations) -- it traces only to text the record never cited, not to the RHS entry actually listed for this field.

records.name_note: The accepted binomial across every admissible source is Wisteria sinensis. NC State Extension titles its page "Wisteria sinensis (Chinese Wisteria, Wisteria)" and RHS's own "Name Status" field for this exact taxon reads "Correct." No admissible source proposes a different accepted name or flags a synonym conflict. Per the task's species note, Wisteria sinensis (Chinese Wisteria) is documented separately from the North American native Wisteria frutescens (American Wisteria) -- NC State Extension maintains a distinct species page for W. frutescens and states there that "American wisteria is not as aggressive a spreader as Wisteria sinensis (Chinese wisteria)." No admissible source conflates the two, and every citation below was checked to confirm it specifically names sinensis (not frutescens or floribunda).
unknowns: toxicity_detail is deliberately thin: NC State Extension structures its poison data as two separate tag blocks -- a 'Problems:' list (which includes 'Problem for Cats,' 'Problem for Dogs,' 'Problem for Horses') and a separate 'Poisonous to Humans:' block (Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: vomiting sometimes with blood, diarrhea, depression; Poison Toxic Principle: lectin, wisterin glycoside; Poison Part: bark, flowers, leaves, roots, sap/juice, seeds, stems). Because the detailed severity/symptom/toxic-principle/plant-part data is nested specifically under the human-only header, it was not used to populate toxicity_detail for pets. RHS is the only source with pet-specific wording ('Pets: Harmful if eaten') and gives no symptom or mechanism detail beyond that phrase.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives ambient day or night temperature targets -- this is a hardy outdoor landscape vine (USDA zones 5a-8b per NC State; RHS Hardiness H6) never described in indoor-temperature terms.

chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives a damage-onset cold temperature. Only survival-oriented hardiness data exists (NC State USDA zones 5a-8b; Missouri Botanical Garden zone 5-8; RHS Hardiness H6, -20 to -15°C), which per the task's own guidance should not be mapped onto a damage-onset field. Missouri Botanical Garden separately notes the plant's 'vulnerability to late spring frost damage to flower buds' but gives no temperature figure for that damage.

Invasive-species concern (no dedicated schema field): multiple admissible sources flag Wisteria sinensis as invasive/regulated outside cultivation. NC State Extension states 'This plant is an invasive species in North Carolina' and describes 'rampant growth and invasive tendency.' Missouri Botanical Garden states the plant 'is listed as a noxious weed in one or more Midwestern states outside Missouri and should not be moved or grown under conditions that would involve danger of dissemination' and separately notes it 'Can be invasive (rampant growth plus rooting surface runners).' Clemson HGIC states 'Chinese wisteria (Wisteria sinensis) is a highly invasive vine and should not be planted in the landscape,' appearing on the 'South Carolina Exotic Pest Plant Council Invasive Plant List.' University of Maryland Extension reports the Maryland Department of Agriculture designates it a 'Tier 2' invasive under a law making 'these three Asian species of wisteria...prohibited under Maryland law,' with populations 'as far south as Louisiana and as far west as Wisconsin.' Penn State Extension calls it an 'introduced invasive vine' and separately states 'the seeds are poisonous.' toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The field's value embeds NC State's human-toxicity-section specifics verbatim -- 'Poison Severity ("Low") / Symptoms ("Vomiting (sometimes with blood), diarrhea, depression") / Toxic Principle ("Lectin, wisterin glycoside")' -- inside a field that is supposed to describe toxicity to PETS. Wrapping it in a disclaimer ('was deliberately not carried into this pet-facing field') doesn't stop the human clinical symptom/mechanism data from sitting in the toxicity_detail text itself; a consumer of this field is exposed to human-scoped poisoning detail as if it were relevant pet context. This is exactly the human-vs-animal-toxicity contamination the audit's check 3 warns about, just achieved through a disclaimer rather than a direct copy. Separately, none of that quoted NC State language ('Poison Severity: Low', the symptom list, 'Lectin, wisterin glycoside') appears anywhere in the citations array -- citation #5's quote is only the bare tag line 'Problems: Invasive Species Problem for Cats Problem for Dogs Problem for Horses Weedy' -- so this portion of the field fails citation-traceability (check 1) independent of the scoping problem. The one genuinely pet-scoped, cited fact ('Pets: Harmful if eaten' from RHS) is sound on its own, but the field as authored goes well beyond it.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The value 'moderate' does not match the actual drainage language in its own citation. Citation #9's quote reads 'slightly acidic, humusy, moderately fertile, medium moisture, well-drained soils' -- the word 'moderately' there modifies FERTILITY, not drainage, and the quote's actual drainage descriptor is 'well-drained.' 'Moderate' appears to be a mapping error (borrowing 'moderately fertile' or 'medium moisture' language onto the wrong attribute). This is compounded by a second admissible source the record itself is aware of: its own unknowns text cites NC State's explicit 'Soil Drainage: Good Drainage, Moist' tag, which also does not say 'moderate' -- both available sources describe drainage as good/well-drained, and neither was reconciled with or cited in support of the chosen 'moderate' value.

unknowns — removed on audit: The invasive-species paragraph in unknowns attributes specific, quotation-styled claims to Clemson HGIC ('highly invasive vine and should not be planted in the landscape'), University of Maryland Extension ('Tier 2', 'prohibited under Maryland law', the Louisiana/Wisconsin range), and Penn State Extension ('introduced invasive vine', 'the seeds are poisonous') -- but none of these three sources appear anywhere in the citations array: no URL, no independently checkable quote entry. I independently verified all three via web search and found the substance accurate (including confirming the Penn State 'seeds are poisonous' line actually describes 'Japanese and Chinese wisteria species' collectively, which does still cover sinensis by name), but the record itself provides no way to verify any of it -- a real citation-traceability gap on a populated field, per the audit's structural check 1.

records.name_note: NC State Extension, Missouri Botanical Garden, Clemson HGIC, and RHS's own separate advice page ("Hibiscus rosa-sinensis | RHS Advice," Botanical name field) all independently use the plain binomial "Hibiscus rosa-sinensis" as this species' working/accepted name. However, RHS's Plant Profile / Find a Plant database entry for the same taxon (rhs.org.uk/plants/8738) titles the page "Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis," gives "Name Status: Correct" for that hybrid-marked form, and lists plain "Hibiscus rosa-sinensis 'Rose of China'" only as a Synonym -- disagreeing with RHS's own growing-guide page on the same domain. Missouri Botanical Garden's profile separately notes "No wild populations of this plant have been found in modern times... This name is often applied to hybrid tropical hibiscus cultivars, although it does not fully reflect the multiple species involved in breeding modern hybrid cultivars," consistent with genuine unresolved ambiguity over whether this taxon is a true species or an ancient hybrid complex. Because RHS's two admissible pages disagree with each other and no admissible source resolves it, scientific_name_accepted is kept equal to the given binomial rather than confidently endorsed as verified; the underlying nomenclature (plain epithet vs. × nothospecies marker) should be treated as unresolved.
records.cool_rest_note: RHS: in cool winter conditions plants overwinter in a semi-dormant state indoors -- flower buds and leaves yellow and drop when indoor light levels are low, but the plant survives this semi-dormant period if watering is reduced (and feeding is stopped).
unknowns: chill_damage_f: genuine conflict between admissible sources, all naming H. rosa-sinensis specifically. UF/IFAS: "Tropical hibiscus requires very high amounts of sunlight and is intolerant to temperatures below 50°F." Clemson: "Bring Chinese hibiscus indoors when nighttime temperatures fall into the lower 50s °F." RHS: "a minimum night temperature of 7ºC (45ºF)" is what cultivation "requires," and its Hardiness quick-fact reads "Tender minimum 7-10ºC (45-50ºF)." The two US extension sources cluster near 50°F while RHS gives 45°F as the minimum required night temperature -- a 5°F disagreement on the same actionable cold-damage question -- so per policy the field is left null rather than picking a side.

day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives a clean ambient day/night temperature range. Only overwintering/cold-tolerance minimums were found, and those themselves conflict: Missouri Botanical Garden says plants "should be overwintered in 60 degree F. locations," while RHS's overwintering guidance calls "minimum night temperatures of 7-10ºC (45-50ºF)" ideal for a glasshouse -- a materially different number for the same concept, so neither was mapped to night_f_min.

USDA Plant Hardiness Zone (NC State: "9a, 9b, 10a, 10b, 11a, 11b"; MOBOT: "Zone: 9 to 11") is a winter-survival zone rating, not a frost-damage-onset temperature, so it was not mapped to chill_damage_f.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: RHS's species profile gives only a categorical value ("pH: Acid or Neutral"), with no numeric range from any admissible source, so left null rather than guess bounds for the category.

soil_drainage: NC State ("Soil Drainage: Good Drainage / Moist"), Missouri Botanical Garden ("moist, organically rich, well-drained soils"), Clemson ("rich, well-drained soil with plenty of organic matter"), and RHS ("Moisture: Well-drained") all combine 'well-drained' with 'moist'/'organically rich' language, but none uses the schema's literal fast/moderate/moisture_retentive wording for this species. Consistent with how this catalog has treated the same ambiguous 'well-drained + moist' combination elsewhere (forcing it to 'moderate' was rejected on audit for a different species on the same grounds), left null rather than force a category.

soil_base: set to 'standard_potting' based specifically on RHS's houseplant/container compost recommendation (peat-free houseplant compost or John Innes No 2). This describes the houseplant/container growing medium. For in-ground zone 9-11 garden cultivation, NC State/MOBOT/Clemson describe soil only qualitatively (rich, organically amended, well-drained) and none names a specific outdoor soil-mix category such as 'garden_bed', so only the container/houseplant medium is captured by this field.

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail: no admissible source (NC State Plant Toolbox, Clemson HGIC, Missouri Botanical Garden, RHS) addresses toxicity of Hibiscus rosa-sinensis to pets, other animals, or humans. NC State's Plant Toolbox Attributes section for this species carries no 'Poison' field at all, and RHS's Plant Profile page -- which does carry a 'Potentially harmful' pet-toxicity field on other species profiles (e.g. it flags Vitis vinifera as harmful to dogs) -- has no such field on this species' page either. Left null rather than inferred as safe.

water_check_depth_cm/water_dry_down_target/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: no admissible source gives a watering frequency in days, a moisture-check depth, or a specific dry-down target. Sources describe watering only qualitatively: 'roots should be kept moist' / 'never dry out' (NC State, MOBOT) during the growing season, versus RHS's instruction to 'Reduce watering as growth slows and only water when the top layer of compost is dry' during winter dormancy -- a seasonal qualitative split, not a day-count or depth figure, so none of these fields could be populated.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: RHS states to 'Begin feeding weekly with a balanced liquid fertiliser for houseplants, about six to eight weeks after repotting' (repotting itself done 'in February or early March'), which names a frequency word ('weekly') and a feeding-start offset but never an explicit calendar month range for the whole feeding window, and never a liquid dilution 'strength' (full/half/quarter). Per policy the only permitted word-to-number translation is a named month to its calendar number for fertilize_active_months, not a frequency word ('weekly') to a day-count, so fertilize_interval_days was left null rather than convert 'weekly' to 7. UF/IFAS separately mentions 'biweekly applications of N-P-K fertilizer' for commercial South Florida field nursery production, but 'biweekly' is itself ambiguous in English (twice-weekly vs. every-two-weeks) and describes a different (commercial outdoor nursery) context than home/houseplant care, so it was not used either.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: no admissible source gives a footcandle value or an upper-bound sun-hours figure for this species; NC State's 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' is a floor, not a ceiling, and RHS's indoor guidance ('bright, filtered light,' 'protected from direct sunlight') is qualitative only.
humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no admissible source gives a numeric humidity percentage; only qualitative categories/instructions are given.

humidity_need: set to 'high' based on NC State ('Chinese hibiscus appreciates high humidity') and Missouri Botanical Garden ('Plants appreciate consistent moisture and high humidity'). RHS's Plant Profile page's generic Cultivation blurb instead says 'moderate humidity,' but that blurb explicitly directs readers to a separate 'Hibiscus rosa-sinensis cultivation' page for species-specific advice, and that dedicated RHS growing guide instead calls for actively increasing humidity via damp gravel trays and describes 'humid conditions' as a requirement -- consistent with 'high' rather than contradicting it. This narrower RHS profile wording was not treated as a controlling conflict given the stronger, more specific corroboration elsewhere.

scientific_name_accepted: see name_note -- RHS's own two admissible pages disagree on whether the correct name carries a × (hybrid) marker; the given plain binomial is retained here because it is what NC State, MOBOT, Clemson, and RHS's own growing-guide page all independently use, but this should be treated as unresolved rather than confidently verified.

outdoor_sun_exposure: 'part_sun' was not used; NC State's category is literally labeled 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours),' mapped to 'part_shade' per this catalog's established convention for that exact phrase.

records.name_note: RHS's own species page carries a structured "Name Status: Correct" field under Botanical Details for Phyllostachys aurea, which this record treats as an affirmative statement of current taxonomic acceptance -- unlike a bare synonym list, which this catalog does not treat as sufficient on its own (see the Rosa rugosa precedent in b20-common-ornamentals.json, where a "Previously known as" list alone was ruled not to establish acceptance). Both NC State ("Previously known as: Phyllostachys breviligula, Phyllostachys formosana") and RHS ("Synonyms: Bambusa aurea, Phyllostachys aurea formosana") separately list historical/synonym names, none of which conflict with or displace Phyllostachys aurea as the current name. This is true bamboo, a woody grass in the Poaceae family (NC State: "Family: Poaceae"; RHS: "Family Poaceae") -- distinct from "Lucky Bamboo," already cataloged in this database under Dracaena sanderiana, which is not a grass and not related. This is the same kind of common-name mismatch already documented elsewhere in this catalog for Sago Palm (not a true palm) and Mini Monstera (not a Monstera).

RHS rates it 'H5: hardy in most places throughout the UK even in severe winters (-15 to -10)' [Celsius] -- a winter-survival hardiness category, not a damage-onset figure. NC State's USDA Hardiness Zone list (4a-10b) is likewise a survival-zone classification, not a stated temperature. UGA's 'Growing Bamboo in Georgia' gives 'Minimum Temp - 0 F' but only for the named variety Phyllostachys aurea holochrysa ('Golden Golden'), not the straight species this record covers, and that figure is itself a minimum-survival temperature rather than a damage-onset one -- so it fails on both counts and was not used.

direct_sun_hours_max: NC State's '6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day' defines the minimum threshold for its 'Full sun' category, not a stated maximum for this species -- the same reasoning already applied elsewhere in this catalog (e.g. Rugosa Rose, b20-common-ornamentals.json) for the identical quote.

soil_ph_min, soil_ph_max: RHS gives pH as 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' -- essentially the full range with no numeric bounds stated -- and no other admissible source gives a pH number for this species.

soil_drainage moderate: this is a categorical inference, not a literal enum term from either source. NC State's tags ('Good Drainage', 'Occasionally Dry', 'Occasionally Wet') describe tolerance of swings in both directions around a well-drained baseline, and RHS's Cultivation text calls for 'moist but well-drained soil.' Neither source uses the words 'fast', 'moderate', or 'moisture retentive'; 'moderate' was chosen as the closest fit to the NC State tolerate-both-ways combination, consistent with how this catalog has mapped similarly ambiguous NC State drainage-tag combinations elsewhere (see the audited soil_drainage note on Rhaphidophora tetrasperma in b22-aroid-genus-gaps.json).

water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis: no admissible source frames watering for this species in container-style regime terms. UGA's 'Growing Bamboo in Georgia' states 'bamboo needs about 1 inch of water every seven to 10 days' and 'A soil pH of 6 to 6.5 is desirable' under a general 'Ground Preparation for Groves' section that applies across the many bamboo genera and species discussed in that document (Bambusa, Chimonobambusa, Phyllostachys, Pseudosasa, Sasa, Sinobambusa), not stated as this species' specific value, so it was not used, per this catalog's rule against presenting genus/class-level figures as a species-specific value.

fertilize_active_months, fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_strength: RHS's only fertilizing instruction for this species ('In a container grow in a peat-free, loam-based compost and feed with a balanced liquid fertiliser on a monthly basis during the growing season') is explicitly scoped to container culture; the same Cultivation paragraph's ground-planting instruction ('Grow in fertile, humus-rich, moist but well-drained soil...') has no fertilizing guidance at all. Since this record treats the species as an outdoor/ground landscape plant (is_houseplant=false), and this catalog has already established (see the audited eggplant/Aubergine fertilize_interval_days finding in b10-veg-round3.json) that container-scoped RHS feeding language should not be force-fit onto a general fertilize field without carrying the container caveat, it was not used here. 'During the growing season' also names no specific months, and 'balanced liquid fertiliser' states no dilution strength.

is_houseplant: RHS's Cultivation section does include container-growing instructions ('In a container grow in a peat-free, loam-based compost...') and lists 'Patio and container plants' among 'Suggested planting locations and garden types' -- but this describes an outdoor patio container, not indoor houseplant culture, and sits alongside outdoor-only guidance (full sun/partial shade position, south- or west-facing aspect, 'protect from cold drying winds', RHS hardiness H5). No admissible source supports growing this species indoors long-term, so is_houseplant is recorded as false rather than left null.

Habit/growth-form conflict found on NC State's own page: its 'Quick ID Hints' list tags this species 'Clump forming bamboo', but the same page's own description paragraph states 'This plant spreads aggressively by rhizomes and will form large stands preventing native plants to grow' and separately lists it as invasive. Every other admissible source addressing growth habit agrees with the rhizome-spreading/running characterization and disagrees with the 'clump forming' tag: RHS's genus note ('Phyllostachys are attractive, large, evergreen bamboos with running rhizomes') and its species-specific Cultivation caveat ('May remain clump-forming in poor or dry soils but can become invasive in warm, moist or favourable conditions'); Clemson HGIC ('Running bamboos can be problematic once established, as they spread by thick, tough, underground stems called rhizomes'); and UMD ('Golden bamboo spreads through underground rhizomes which grow quickly, spreading out horizontally from the parent plant'). NC State's 'Clump forming bamboo' Quick ID tag was treated as an unreliable outlier that contradicts its own page's prose and was not used for any field.

Running-bamboo containment and invasiveness (no dedicated field in this schema, captured here per task instructions because it materially affects whether a home gardener should plant this species directly in the ground): this is a running, rhizome-spreading bamboo, not a clumping one. The South Carolina Exotic Plant Pest Council designates it 'a severe environmental threat' capable of being 'highly detrimental to the composition, structure, and function of natural areas from South Carolina's Piedmont through the Coastal Plain' (Clemson HGIC, Bamboo Control factsheet). NC State lists it as invasive in North Carolina; UMD reports it is 'now considered an invasive species in Maryland, Pennsylvania, Virginia, West Virginia and Georgia'; Penn State Extension's 'Don't Plant a Pest' fact sheet lists 'Golden bamboo - Phyllostachys aurea' among its partial list of invasive plants; and RHS's own species page cautions it 'can become invasive in warm, moist or favourable conditions.' Rhizomes are hard to contain: Clemson says they 'can spread more than 100 feet from the mother plant and are very resistant to adverse environmental conditions and most herbicides'; UMD similarly says rhizomes 'allow the plant to spread for a hundred or more feet in any unobstructed direction' and 'can run indefinitely unless damaged at the growing tip.' Physical barriers only redirect rather than stop growth and need ongoing upkeep: Clemson recommends a barrier 'made of concrete, metal, high density polyethylene (HDPE), or pressure-treated wood installed about 18 inches deep' but warns 'bamboo rhizomes are not stopped by barriers but are merely reflected,' so surrounding areas must be 'monitored regularly'; UMD specifies barrier material of 'a minimum thickness of 60 mil... polypropylene [PP] or high-density polyethylene [HDPE]' installed so 'About 6 to 8 inches of the barrier should remain above-ground,' warning 'Any break in the barrier can allow rhizomes to spread undetected.' For an already-established stand, UMD says 'all rhizomes must be removed through excavation' and 'repeated treatment of the area will likely be necessary to ensure complete eradication.' Given this, a home gardener considering this species should plan for a permanent physical barrier plus ongoing monitoring, or grow it in a large container instead of directly in open ground.

Chinese Hibiscus landed with toxic_to_pets correctly null after a genuinely thorough four-source search found no toxicity data at all for this species -- not assumed toxic by Malvaceae-family association, not assumed safe by silence. Golden Bamboo (Phyllostachys aurea) continues this catalog's running theme of common-name naming traps -- true bamboo (a grass, Poaceae), unrelated to "Lucky Bamboo" (Dracaena sanderiana, already covered) the way Sago Palm isn't a true palm and Mini Monstera isn't a Monstera. It's also a running, rhizome-spreading, invasive-listed species in multiple states -- captured at length in unknowns even though the schema has no dedicated field for it, since it materially affects whether a home gardener should plant it directly in the ground versus in a contained pot.
